'''Luana Reyes''' (February 20, 1933<ref>Date of birth as per the Social Security Death Index (SSDI)</ref> – November 5, 2001<ref name="A Tribute… 2002">"A Tribute…" 2002</ref>) was an [[Native Americans in the United States|American Indian]] health care administrator. As executive director of the [[Seattle Indian Health Board]] (SIHB) 1972–1982, she grew that institution from a staff of five to nearly 200 and made it a model for [[urban Indian]] institutions; subsequently, she worked for the federal [[Indian Health Service]], eventually becoming deputy director of that 14,000-person institution.<ref>Reyes 2002, pp. 185–86.</ref><ref>Reyes 2002 gives her title as "assistant director", but the July 1999 [http://www.ncai.org/ncai/resource/documents/governance/CSCfinalrep.htm Final Report] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061201192014/https://www.ncai.org/ncai/resource/documents/governance/CSCfinalrep.htm |date=2006-12-01 }} of the National Congress of American Indians National Policy Work Group on Contract Support Costs (accessed online March 11, 2007)
gives it as Deputy Director, as does [http://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/prof/heart/other/aianwksp/aianwksp.pdf Summary Report for the “Mobilizing American Indian and Alaska Native Communities Workshop on Improving Cardiovascular Health”, National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute — Indian Health Board Partnership] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070609215900/http://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/prof/heart/other/aianwksp/aianwksp.pdf |date=2007-06-09 }}, May 7–8, 2001 (accessed online March 11, 2007) and other similar official documents.</ref>

On October 10, 2001, shortly before her death from  [[aplastic anemia]] at the age of 68, she received the Presidential Rank Meritorious Award.<ref>"A Tribute…" 2002; Reyes 2002, p. 186</ref><ref name=Green-2001>[https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/20011110/obit10m/luana-reyes-68-a-leader-in-agency-for-indian-health Green 2001].</ref>

==Life==
Reyes was born in Portland, Oregon.<ref name=Green-2001 /> Her mother, born Mary Christian, was [[Sin Aikst]] (now known as Lakes tribe, one of the Confederated Tribes of the [[Colville Indian Reservation|Colville Reservation]]); her father, Julian Reyes, was [[Philippines|Filipino]], but had largely assimilated to an Indian way of life. Her mother's father, Alex Christian, was known as ''Pic Ah Kelowna,'' "White Grizzly Bear"; her great-uncle (brother of her maternal grandmother) was Chief [[James Bernard (chief)|James Bernard]], a Sin Aikst leader in the early 20th century.<ref>Reyes 2002, p. 28–50.</ref>

Reyes' early childhood was spent largely on the [[Colville Indian Reservation]] in [[Washington (U.S. state)|Washington]]. In 1935–1937, during the period of construction of the [[Grand Coulee Dam]], her parents had moved to the Coulee and started a Chinese restaurant even though "[n]either of them could prepare Chinese food except for simple dishes such as pork fried rice, egg foo-yung, and chop suey". They soon acquired an ethnically Chinese partner and cook, Harry Wong; Wong bought them out of the restaurant in 1937.<ref>Reyes 2002, pp. 74–75.</ref> Her parents separated in 1939 and subsequently divorced;<ref>Reyes 2002, p. 90.</ref> her mother would later work again for Wong in [[Tacoma, Washington]], and eventually marry him.<ref>Reyes 2002, pp. 185, 194.</ref>

From 1940 to 1942, Reyes and her older brother Lawney were students at the [[Chemawa Indian School]] five miles north of [[Salem, Oregon]]<ref>Reyes 2002, ''passim.''</ref> After graduating at the head of her class<ref>Reyes 2006, p. 52</ref> from Okanogan High School ([[Okanogan, Washington]]) in 1951, she moved to [[Tacoma, Washington]], living with her mother, working in a department store and for Harry Wong's restaurant.<ref name="Reyes 2002, p. 185">Reyes 2002, p. 185.</ref> She worked over the next twenty years in the private sector in [[San Francisco]], [[Hawaii]], and [[Seattle, Washington|Seattle]] before succeeding her younger brother, activist [[Bernie Whitebear]], as executive director of the Seattle Indian Health Board, which, over the next decade she transformed from a tiny organization with a staff of five <ref>Reyes 2002, p. 185, 187.</ref> into "a comprehensive community health care center with a multimillion-dollar budget and over 190 full-time health professionals and support staff."<ref name="A Tribute… 2002"/> During this time, she helped to found the American Indian Health Care Association, now known as the [[National Council on Urban Indian Health]].<ref name="A Tribute… 2002"/> Subsequently, after a brief stint as executive director of the [[Puyallup Nation]] Health Authority community health program,<ref name="A Tribute… 2002"/> she worked at the headquarters of the federal Indian Health Service ([[Rockville, Maryland]]), eventually becoming director of headquarters operations, chief financial officer, and deputy director of that 14,000-person institution.<ref name="A Tribute… 2002"/><ref>Reyes 2002, pp. 185–86, but see note above on the title "deputy director".</ref><ref>For "director of headquarters operations" see [https://www.senate.gov/~scia/1998hrgs/1007_lr.pdf Reyes' testimony] before the Indian Affairs Committee of the U.S. Senate, October 7, 1998, regarding tribal self-governance and healthcare. Accessed online March 11, 2007</ref><ref>For "chief financial officer" see [https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/20011110/obit10m/luana-reyes-68-a-leader-in-agency-for-indian-health Green 2001].</ref>

==Family==
She had one child, a daughter, Kecia, born in 1985.<ref name="Reyes 2002, p. 185"/> Reyes' brother, Bernie Whitebear (1937–2000), was a prominent activist, not only founder of SIHB, but co-founder of the [[United Indians of All Tribes Foundation]], and the [[Daybreak Star Cultural Center]]; her older brother [[Lawney Reyes]] is a sculptor, designer, curator, and memoirist.<ref>Reyes 2002, ''passim'', especially p. 181 ''et. seq.''</ref>

==Legacy==
There is now a Luana Reyes Leadership Award named in her honor.<ref>"Other News", [http://www.navajo.org/images/pdf%20releases/KFrancisPR/dec06/Navajo%20Nation%20Council%20overrides%20veto%20of%20funds%20for%20Chapters,%20passes%20Legislation%20to%20establish%20Navajo%20Code%20Talkers%20Day_Dec22.pdf press release], Karen Francis, Public Information Officer, Navajo Nation Council Office of the Speaker, December 22, 2006. Accessed online March 11, 2007.</ref>

The Reyes Building located at 801 Thompson Avenue, Rockville, Maryland is named in her honor.
